teaser: A small blue hippo, sealed in a tomb shaft and never meant to be seen by anyone alive.
review_notes:
IMAGE MISMATCH: the catalog image shows a dark bronze/copper-alloy hippopotamus statuette with green corrosion, not the Met's blue faience hippo 'William' (accession 17.9.1). The lesson text describes William; the single interactive block points only at the general shape of the animal in the current image and must be redone once the correct image is in place.
Tomb attribution: shaft of the tomb chapel of the steward Senbi (II) at Meir, excavated 1910; Met purchase 1917.
Punch article by Captain H. M. Raleigh, 18 March 1931; reprinted in the Met Bulletin the same year.
Three of the four legs are modern restorations (Met).
Size about 20 cm long, 11 cm high.

lesson.text: Meir, Middle Egypt, around 1900 BC. A shaft is cut straight down into the desert rock beside the tomb chapel of a steward named Senbi. At the bottom, next to the coffin, someone sets down a hippopotamus about the length of a hand. Then the shaft is filled in. The little animal is meant for darkness, and for one viewer only: the dead man.

That hippo is the one New Yorkers call William. He is about 20 cm long (8 inches) and bright blue-green, with river plants painted in black lines across his back and sides: lotus buds, open lotus flowers, leaves. It is as if you were seeing the animal through the marsh it lives in.

The picture attached to this lesson is not William. It shows a dark metal hippo statuette, with no blue glaze and no painted flowers. Use it for the animal's shape only, and keep in mind that the real William is the color of a swimming pool.

Why bury a hippo with a man you loved? To Egyptians the animal had two faces. It was among the most dangerous creatures on the Nile, able to overturn a boat and crush a field of crops in a night. It also sank under the water and rose again each morning, which made it a sign of rebirth.

The lotus painted on William says the same thing in flowers. A lotus closes at night and opens again with the sun. So the tomb held a small machine for coming back to life: an animal that resurfaces, wrapped in a plant that reopens.
An Egyptian tomb object is not decoration. It is equipment, placed there to do a job for the dead in the next life.

But a helper this dangerous needed a safety catch. A statue, in Egyptian thinking, could become the thing it showed. A hippo loose in the afterlife might attack its owner. The answer was simple and brutal, and it concerns the part of the animal that touches the ground.

lesson.title: Shape of a hippo
lesson.text: This stand-in statuette has the same build as William. Two places matter for his story.

spots.title: Four short legs
spots.text: Before burial, William's legs were snapped off on purpose so he could not charge. Three of the four you see on him at the Met today are modern replacements.

spots.title: The heavy head
spots.text: Egyptian makers kept the head low and broad, eyes and ears set high, the way a hippo looks when only the top of its skull breaks the surface of the river.

lesson.text: So the animal you meet in the museum has been repaired against the wishes of the people who buried him. They wanted him crippled. We wanted him whole. It is a small reminder that museums change what objects mean.

His body is not clay and not stone. It is Egyptian faience: ground quartz mixed with a little lime and plant ash, shaped by hand, then fired. In the kiln the surface melts into a glassy skin, and a pinch of copper turns it blue-green. Egyptians called the material by a word meaning “dazzling”.

He got his name from a joke. In 1931 the British magazine Punch printed a story by Captain H. M. Raleigh, whose family kept a color print of the Met's hippo on the wall, called it William, and consulted its expression before making decisions.

The museum reprinted the story, and the name stuck for good. The hippo had entered the collection in 1917. Since then he has become its unofficial mascot, copied as toys, mugs and children's books. A tomb guard for one Egyptian official now greets millions of strangers.

He was not alone. Blue hippos like him were placed in many tombs of the same period, and several museums own one. What makes this one famous is partly his quality, the even glaze and the confident drawing, and partly the luck of a good nickname.
William was made to be dangerous, then disarmed, then buried. Almost 4,000 years later he was dug up, mended and given a pet name. Each age has made a different animal of him.

quiz.question: Where was William placed around 1900 BC?
options: In a tomb shaft at Meir, beside a coffin
quiz.explanation: He was set down in the burial shaft of the steward Senbi's tomb at Meir.

quiz.question: Why were his legs broken before burial?
options: So he could not harm the dead man in the afterlife
To make him fit inside the coffin
They broke by accident in the kiln
quiz.explanation: A statue could become what it showed, so the hippo was disarmed.

quiz.question: What is Egyptian faience made from?
options: Ground quartz, fired until the surface turns glassy
quiz.explanation: Faience is a quartz-based ceramic, colored blue-green with copper.

quiz.question: What do the lotus flowers painted on him suggest?
options: Rebirth, since the lotus reopens every morning
quiz.explanation: The lotus closes at night and opens with the sun, a sign of rebirth.

quiz.question: Where does the name William come from?
options: A 1931 story in the magazine Punch
quiz.explanation: Captain H. M. Raleigh's family had nicknamed a print of the hippo William.

facts.text: William is carved from blue stone.
facts.explanation: He is modeled in faience, a fired quartz ceramic with a glassy blue-green surface.

facts.text: Most of the legs you see on William today are modern restorations.
facts.explanation: His legs were deliberately broken in antiquity, and three were remade.

facts.text: Ancient Egyptians saw the hippopotamus only as a harmless, friendly animal.
facts.explanation: It was feared as one of the most dangerous animals on the Nile, and also linked to rebirth.
